clue.text: Sour apple with sage to one side?

blocks.note: a crab apple is a small sour wild apple
sage as an adjective means wise

explanation.surface: A cook sets a sour apple and some sage aside on the plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sage' looks like the herb beside the apple, but it is the adjective meaning wise.
explanation.definitionFit: Crabwise means moving sideways, as a crab walks, so it describes going off to one side.

clue.text: Agree difficult condition has no exit

indicators.note: has no means lacking, so a group of letters is taken away

blocks.note: complexity is the state of being difficult or intricate
taken as written

explanation.surface: A difficult term in a contract allows no way out, so you must agree.
explanation.definitionFit: To comply is to go along with a request or rule, a synonym of agree as an intransitive verb.

clue.text: Agreement about holding one: squeeze it while operating keys

indicators.note: something holding another thing has it inside its grip

blocks.note: an accord is an agreement
I is the Roman numeral one
on can mean about, as in a talk on art

explanation.surface: A deal on a shared object comes with instructions to press it while working its buttons.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a playful description: the player squeezes the bellows while pressing the keys.
explanation.definitionFit: An accordion is a bellows instrument played by pumping it in and out while pressing keys or buttons.

clue.text: What’s the future of hospital in decline?

indicators.note: in places one item within the other

blocks.note: H is the map and road-sign abbreviation for hospital
to wither is to shrivel and decline

explanation.surface: A worried question about where a declining hospital is heading.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase: 'Whither the NHS?' asks what lies ahead for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Whither, used in headlines and rhetoric, asks where something is going, that is, what lies ahead for it.

clue.text: Sons are covered by promise

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
what you wear is what you are covered in

explanation.surface: Sons find themselves bound by a pledge.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is loose: 'are covered' stands for WEAR, since clothes you wear cover you.
explanation.definitionFit: To swear is to make a solemn vow, so as a verb it means to promise.

clue.text: Bring back a sample from Austria, homespun cloth

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
a sample is a small piece taken out of something larger, so the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: the end of Austria and the start of homespun run together

explanation.surface: A traveller is asked to bring home a swatch of rustic Austrian homespun fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run backwards across the join of Austria and homespun to spell MOHAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Mohair is a fabric woven from the silky hair of the Angora goat, so it is a kind of cloth.

clue.text: Work about English detective who had parental problems

indicators.note: about means around, so one word surrounds the others

blocks.note: an opus is a work, especially of music
E is the abbreviation for English
DI is a Detective Inspector

explanation.surface: A book about an English detective with a difficult relationship with his parents.
explanation.walkthrough: DI is Detective Inspector, a British police rank.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Oedipus unknowingly killed his father and married his mother, the ultimate parental trouble.

clue.text: Yellowish variety of bream

indicators.note: a variety is a different form of something, so the letters take a new form

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An angler describes a yellowish kind of bream, a freshwater fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Amber is the colour of fossil resin, a warm orange-yellow shade.

clue.text: Bothering to swallow what’s in best wine

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so one word goes within another
what is in a word is its interior, so only its central letters are kept

blocks.note: riling means annoying, bothering
the two central letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone is annoyed into gulping down the best wine on offer.
explanation.definitionFit: Riesling is a white grape variety and the wine made from it, notably in Germany and Alsace.

clue.text: Man with edge of mouth or tip of tongue where choppers may rest

indicators.note: the tip of something is its very front end, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: he is the pronoun for a man
the lip forms the edge of the mouth
taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dentist describes a man's mouth, lips and tongue, where his teeth may sit.
explanation.walkthrough: With mouth, lip and tongue around, 'choppers' suggests teeth; they are helicopters.
explanation.definitionFit: A heliport is an airfield for helicopters, so it is a place where these aircraft land and park.

clue.text: Chap holding part of jaw before an expert for automatic scanning

indicators.note: something holding other things keeps them within its own two ends

blocks.note: a chap is a man, a male
the chin is the front of the lower jaw
ere is an old word for before
a dab, as in dab hand, is an expert

explanation.surface: A man with a jaw injury sees a specialist about a scan.
explanation.walkthrough: The chap's word splits round everything that follows it. A 'dab hand' is a skilled person, so a dab is an expert; ere is archaic for before.
explanation.definitionFit: Data that is machine-readable is in a form a computer can scan and process without human help.

clue.text: Cross from church separating temptation and resistance

indicators.note: something separating a word pushes its letters apart by sitting between them

blocks.note: a lure is a temptation or enticement
CH is the usual abbreviation for church
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Someone is angry after church, caught between temptation and resisting it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry, but it is a noun: a crossbreed, here a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A lurcher is a crossbred dog, typically a greyhound mixed with a collie or terrier, so it is a cross.

clue.text: Expose drive to circumscribe Royal Institution

indicators.note: to circumscribe is to draw a line around, so one word is set around another

blocks.note: to impel is to drive forward
RI is the abbreviation for the Royal Institution, a London scientific body

explanation.surface: A campaign to fence in the Royal Institution threatens to leave it exposed.
explanation.definitionFit: To imperil something is to put it in danger, which is to expose it to harm.

clue.text: Liberal recalled subject of Ring of Bright Water book

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the word that follows is taken back to front

blocks.note: Lib is the short form of Liberal

blocks.clueFragment: subject of Ring of Bright Water
blocks.note: Gavin Maxwell's 1960 memoir Ring of Bright Water is about his pet otters

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician remembers what Gavin Maxwell's famous nature book was about.
explanation.walkthrough: Ring of Bright Water is Gavin Maxwell's well-known memoir of life with otters in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A libretto is the text of an opera or musical, often called its book.

clue.text: One must admit beer’s out after rehabilitation

indicators.note: rehabilitation remakes a person, so these letters are rebuilt in a fresh order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A recovering drinker concedes that beer is off the menu after rehab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One must admit' reads as a confession; it is a concessive phrase like 'admittedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'to be sure' concedes a point before a counter-argument, just as admittedly does.

clue.text: Home for many Arabs and US strays

indicators.note: things that stray wander off their path, so these letters drift into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A country is home to many Arab people, along with some wandering Americans.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudan is an African country whose population is largely Arab, so it is home to many of them.

clue.text: Fail to tour resort with flag run down

indicators.note: touring a place means going all round it, so one word circles the others

blocks.note: an engine that fails dies
a spa is a health resort
a rag is a scruffy flag or banner

explanation.surface: A weary traveller is too exhausted to visit a resort, flagging and run down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' and 'run down' look like tiredness; flag is a noun and 'run down' means to criticise.
explanation.definitionFit: To disparage someone is to belittle them, which is to run them down.

clue.text: I declare a corgi disturbed one’s royal self

indicators.note: something disturbed is jumbled out of place, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
royalty speak of themselves as 'we', so the royal self as object is 'us'

explanation.surface: The Queen exclaims that one of her corgis has upset her.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal 'we' (and so 'us') is the plural a monarch uses for herself.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Gracious!' is an old-fashioned exclamation of surprise, just like 'I declare!'

clue.text: Phoned with no good time for preparation

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so a letter is removed from the phrase

blocks.note: rung up is a British way of saying phoned
G is the usual abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone phoned, but got nowhere good in the time they had to prepare.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain to ring someone up is to phone them; drop the G from RUNG UP.
explanation.definitionFit: The run-up to an event is the period leading up to it, when people get ready.

clue.text: Pupil learning by repetition, good in games

indicators.note: in places one group of letters within another

blocks.note: PE, physical education, is school games
learning by rote is learning by repetition
G is the usual abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A pupil who learns by drilling turns out to be good at sport.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools games lessons are PE, physical education.
explanation.definitionFit: A protégé is someone guided and promoted by a mentor, effectively a pupil.

clue.text: Simply lock for support

blocks.note: but can mean simply or only, as in 'but a child'
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: Just bolt the door if you need something to lean on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' suggests a door bolt; it is a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A buttress is a projecting structure that props up a wall, so it is a support.

clue.text: Perhaps Italian serving king has same name as Bismarck?

blocks.note: R stands for rex, Latin for king
someone who has a name is called it, so he is that name
Otto von Bismarck was the first Chancellor of Germany

explanation.surface: A puzzle about whether an Italian waiter serving a king shares Bismarck's first name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian serving' looks like a waiter; serving is a noun, a portion of food.
explanation.definitionFit: Risotto is an Italian rice dish, so it is an example of an Italian serving of food.

clue.text: Bomb to measure by foot tons over kilometres

indicators.note: over means covering, so one letter is covered by the word next to it

blocks.note: to pace a distance is to measure it in steps
K is short for kilometres
T is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: Engineers plan to pace out the blast range of a bomb, tons over kilometres.
explanation.walkthrough: The placing is loose: K goes inside PACE with T after it. 'Bomb' means a large sum of money: something that costs a bomb costs a packet.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang both a bomb and a packet mean a large amount of money.

clue.text: Chamber’s beguiling invitations when heart’s lost to maiden

indicators.note: the heart is the central letter, and losing it to something means that thing takes its place

blocks.note: come-ons are flirtatious or enticing invitations
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A romantic young woman loses heart when a chamber's seductive invitations reach her.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle letter of COME-ONS is E; swap it for M.
explanation.definitionFit: The Commons, the lower house of the UK Parliament, is one of its two legislative chambers.

clue.text: What galleon wouldn’t need time in dock?

indicators.note: in places one letter within the following word

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to moor a boat is to dock it

explanation.surface: A question about whether a sailing galleon would need time in harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: A galleon is a sailing ship, so it has no engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A galleon runs on sails alone, so an engine is something it would never need.

clue.text: Coat applied to make batting more effective?

definitions.text: Coat applied to make batting more effective?

blocks.clueFragment: Coat applied to make batting more effective?
blocks.note: surface reading: a cricketer treats the bat with a coat of linseed oil before an innings
setter's reading: batting the eyelashes, a flirtatious flutter, made more striking by a coat of eye make-up

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket bats are oiled, so 'batting' points to the game; here it is the fluttering of eyelashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Mascara is a cosmetic brushed onto the eyelashes to darken and thicken them.

clue.text: Shred incorporated in third note

indicators.note: in places one group of letters within the next

blocks.note: me, also spelt mi, is the third note of the sol-fa scale
Inc is the abbreviation for incorporated, used of companies

explanation.surface: A shredded document has been filed into a company's third notice.
explanation.walkthrough: Doh, ray, me: the third note is often spelt ME in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: To mince food is to chop it very finely, close in sense to shredding it.

clue.text: Unlikely to reach a conclusion after missing points?

definitions.text: Unlikely to reach a conclusion after missing points?

blocks.clueFragment: Unlikely to reach a conclusion after missing points?
blocks.note: surface reading: a debater who misses the points of an argument will not reach the right conclusion
setter's reading: railway points, the switches that send a train onto one line or another, so a train that misses them heads off down the wrong line

explanation.walkthrough: Points here are the movable rails at a railway junction; a train sent the wrong way never reaches its terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means mistaken in one's reasoning, from a train running down the wrong line.

clue.text: County doubtless welcoming Republican unknown

indicators.note: welcoming someone means taking them in, so one word goes inside another

blocks.note: doubtless means certain, sure
R is the abbreviation for Republican
in algebra x, y and z stand for unknowns

explanation.surface: A county is said to be certain to welcome an unknown Republican candidate.
explanation.walkthrough: SURREY is a county south-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Surrey is one of the home counties of England, bordering London to the south-west.

clue.text: Strongly suggesting incorporating state benefit into housing expense

indicators.note: incorporating means taking something into the body of something else
into says where the taken-in word ends up, inside the next one

blocks.note: rent is the regular cost of housing
the dole is British slang for state unemployment benefit

explanation.surface: A proposal to fold welfare payments into housing costs is put forward forcefully.
explanation.walkthrough: The dole is everyday British slang for unemployment benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: Redolent means evocative, so a thing redolent of the past calls the past strongly to mind.
